opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. So the core idea behind EMMA was to ask: what happens if you take a model that has already absorbed an enormous amount of world knowledge from internet-scale data, like Gemini, and adapt it end to end for driving? Traditionally, autonomous driving stacks are built from specialized modules trained on driving data alone. That data is rich, but it's narrow. It doesn't necessarily teach a system what a construction worker's hand signal means, or that a mattress lying on the highway is something to avoid, or how to reason about an unusual scene it has never seen before in the fleet logs.

A pretrained multimodal model brings a few things. First, there's the world knowledge and common sense, which helps a lot with the long tail of rare situations that are so hard in driving. Second, there's reasoning ability. In EMMA we experimented with chain-of-thought style prompting, where the model explicitly describes critical objects, the scene, and the intended behavior before producing a trajectory, and we found that this kind of structured reasoning actually improved planning quality. Third, there's a nice unification aspect. Because everything is expressed in a common language-and-vision space, you can train one model to do motion planning, 3D object detection, road graph estimation, and so on, and these tasks can benefit from each other through co-training.

We got quite strong results, including state-of-the-art-level performance on public benchmarks like nuScenes planning and competitive results on the Waymo Open Motion Dataset. That said, I want to be clear that EMMA is a research exploration, not a production system. There are real limitations: these models are expensive to run in real time, the version we studied relied mostly on camera input without lidar, and handling long temporal context remains a challenge. Also, in safety-critical systems you want strong verification, and that's an area where structured, more interpretable intermediate representations still matter a lot.

So I see the value less as "replace everything with one big model" and more as learning how to bring the knowledge and reasoning of these foundation models into the driving stack, whether as a teacher, a component, or eventually something more central, while keeping the rigor that safe driving requires.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So the way I think about it is that driving is, at its core, a problem of understanding the world and then acting in it, and for a long time the field built that understanding from scratch, with purpose-built perception models, behavior prediction models, planners, all trained on driving data that we collected ourselves. That works, and it's gotten us very far, but it means the system only knows what it has seen on the road.

What's interesting about a model like Gemini is that it comes with an enormous amount of world knowledge baked in before it ever sees a driving example. It knows what a school bus is, what a stop sign means, what a police officer waving their arms is likely asking you to do, that a ball rolling into the street might be followed by a child. Those are the kinds of semantic, common-sense things that are really hard to cover exhaustively with a hand-curated driving dataset, because the long tail is just enormous. So with EMMA the question we wanted to ask was: if you take that pretrained model and adapt it to driving, how much of that knowledge actually transfers, and does it help?

And the second piece is the end-to-end aspect. In EMMA we take raw camera input and the model directly outputs things like the future trajectory, as well as perception outputs like object detection and road graph elements, all represented in natural language or as text tokens. That lets you train one model on many driving tasks at once, and we found there's positive transfer between them. Training on perception tasks helps planning, and vice versa, which is a nice property you don't automatically get with a modular stack. It also gives you a form of reasoning. The model can produce a rationale for why it's doing something, which is useful both for interpretability and, in our experiments, actually improved driving quality.

Now, I want to be careful not to oversell it. EMMA was a research exploration, not a production system. There are real limitations: it only handled a small number of frames at a time, it didn't natively consume lidar or radar, which are important for safety, and these models are computationally very expensive to run in a vehicle at the latency you need. So I see the value less as "this replaces the stack tomorrow" and more as evidence that this large body of general knowledge in foundation models is a genuinely powerful prior for driving, and that the recipe for bringing it into the vehicle is something worth investing in seriously.

astra-6.text:
The value is that you’re starting with a model that already has a very broad understanding of the world, rather than learning everything from driving data alone. Driving is full of situations where that broader understanding could be useful—interpreting an unusual object in the road, understanding what a person might be trying to do, or making sense of a scene you haven’t encountered very often in training.

With EMMA, we explored whether we could adapt those capabilities to driving: take camera inputs and a description of the driving task, and train the model to produce a trajectory. That gives us a way to connect the representations learned during large-scale multimodal pretraining to the actual decisions a vehicle needs to make.

Another interesting aspect is bringing different tasks into a common framework. Understanding the scene and planning how to move through it are closely related, and learning them together can potentially help both. The research question is how much of that general knowledge transfers, and where you still need specialized driving data and capabilities. It’s a promising direction, but demonstrating that transfer is only part of the work needed to build a reliable autonomous driving system.

sol-6.1.text:
The big opportunity is to bring the broad knowledge and reasoning capabilities of a model like Gemini into the driving domain. Driving requires more than recognizing objects. You need to understand the context of a scene, interpret what other road users might do, and handle situations that you may not have seen very often in your driving data. Multimodal pretraining gives you a potentially very useful starting point for that.

With EMMA, we explored adapting that foundation to take driving inputs and predict a vehicle’s future trajectory. One interesting aspect is that you can represent different driving tasks within a common language-based framework, which allows you to study how those tasks can benefit one another.

I would view this as a research direction, though. Broad world knowledge is valuable, but translating it into precise, reliable driving behavior is still a substantial challenge. The question is how much that pretrained understanding can help with generalization, particularly in unusual or complex situations.
